equity.level_reason: Screening prevalence is reported by education, wealth, caste/tribe, religion and rurality with chi-square tests and described as associations, but contrasts are side-by-side values and ranges with no computed difference or ratio, and no disparity framing.

ev.q: Weighted prevalence estimates of women who reported screening and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.
Among women in India aged 30–49 years, less than one third (29.8%) reported ever having been screened for cervical cancer.
Age group (yrs) › 30–34
When assessed by household wealth, prevalence was lowest among women from the poorest households (17.1%) and highest among those from the wealthiest households (40.4%).
Screening prevalence increased with women’s educational level and that of their partners, ranging from 24.7% among women with no formal education
screening prevalence was higher among women in urban (34.0%) than among those in rural (27.5%) areas
lower among women who belonged to a Scheduled Tribe (25.1%) or Scheduled Caste (28.2%) than among women in “Other Backward Classes” (30.8%)
Screening prevalences were lower among Hindu (29.4%) and Muslim (26.8%) women than among Sikh (50.2%), Buddhist (48.2%), and Christian (39.1%) women
it is important to consider how socioeconomic factors might be associated with acceptance of screening at the district, state, and national levels.
